subject: Environment
topic: Climate summits and agreements — mixed tiers

questions.stem: The landmark 1992 Earth Summit — at which the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was signed — was held at:

options.option_text: Stockholm
Rio de Janeiro
Johannesburg
Paris

questions.explanation: The 1992 Earth Summit was held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The UNFCCC (climate), CBD (biodiversity) and the Forest Principles all came out of this summit. Stockholm — 1972, the first major world environment conference (UNEP was created as a follow-up). Johannesburg — 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development (Rio+10). Rio+20 — Rio again, 2012.

questions.stem: The Kyoto Protocol, which committed developed countries to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, was adopted in:
questions.explanation: Kyoto Protocol — adopted at COP-3 in December 1997, entered into force in 2005. Mandatory emission-reduction targets only for developed ('Annex I') countries in its first commitment period (2008-12). The US never ratified it. Its successor — the Paris Agreement, adopted at COP-21 in December 2015, involves every country. The 1987 Montreal Protocol is a separate treaty — about ozone-layer-depleting substances, not climate change.

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep the long-term rise in global average temperature below:

options.option_text: 1°C above pre-industrial levels
2°C (with an aspiration of 1.5°C) above pre-industrial levels
3°C above pre-industrial levels
5°C above pre-industrial levels

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement (COP-21) aims to limit warming to 'well below 2 °C' and to pursue efforts to keep it to 1.5 °C relative to pre-industrial (1850-1900) temperature. Each country submits NDCs (Nationally Determined Contributions), updated every 5 years. India's updated NDC (2022) — reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45 % from 2005 level by 2030; 50 % of electricity from non-fossil sources by 2030. Net-zero target — 2070.

questions.stem: The IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) was established in:

options.option_text: 1972 by UNEP
1988 by WMO and UNEP
1992 by the Rio Summit
2005 by the Kyoto Protocol

questions.explanation: IPCC — set up in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) to assess the science of climate change. Its reports (Assessment Reports AR1 to AR6, Special Reports like the 1.5 °C Report) underpin UNFCCC negotiations. Nobel Peace Prize 2007 (shared with Al Gore). Headquartered in Geneva. Does not do original research — synthesises existing science.

questions.stem: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is primarily about the phase-out of substances that deplete:

options.option_text: The greenhouse gases
The ozone layer
The acid-rain pollutants
Persistent organic pollutants

questions.explanation: Montreal Protocol (1987) — phases out CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride etc. Credited as the most successful international environmental treaty; the ozone hole is measurably healing. The Kigali Amendment (2016) added phase-down of HFCs (which do not harm ozone but are potent greenhouse gases). Stockholm Convention (2001) — POPs. UNFCCC/Kyoto/Paris — climate change.

questions.stem: COP-26 (2021), the climate summit that produced the 'Glasgow Climate Pact', was hosted by:

options.option_text: Germany
United Kingdom (Glasgow)
Egypt
United Arab Emirates

questions.explanation: COP-26 — Glasgow, UK, 2021. India announced 'Panchamrit' (five pillars) — 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030, 50 % of energy from renewables, 1 GT emission cuts, intensity -45 %, net-zero by 2070. COP-27 — Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022) — Loss-and-Damage fund agreed. COP-28 — Dubai, UAE (2023) — first global stocktake + 'transitioning away from fossil fuels' in the agreed text.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most abundant human-generated greenhouse gas by volume in Earth's atmosphere?

options.option_text: Methane
Carbon dioxide
Nitrous oxide
HFC-134a

questions.explanation: CO₂ — dominant human-emitted greenhouse gas, ~420 ppm in 2024 (pre-industrial ~280 ppm). Methane — more potent per molecule (about 25× over 100 years) but at much lower concentration (~1,900 ppb). N₂O, SF₆ and HFCs are tiny fractions but can be long-lived and potent. Water vapour is the largest natural GHG but responds to temperature rather than driving it directly.

questions.stem: The Secretariat of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which coordinates global climate negotiations, is permanently headquartered in which city?

options.option_text: Geneva, Switzerland — seat of WHO and WTO headquarters
Bonn, Germany — permanent UNFCCC Secretariat host since 1996
New York, USA — principal headquarters of the United Nations
Nairobi, Kenya — host of UNEP and UN-Habitat global offices

questions.explanation: B is correct: the UNFCCC Secretariat relocated from Geneva to Bonn in 1996 at the invitation of Germany and has remained there since. Geneva (A) hosts WHO and WTO — a common confusion. Nairobi (D) hosts UNEP, which is a different UN body. New York hosts UN Headquarters but not the UNFCCC Secretariat.

questions.stem: The Kigali Amendment (2016) to the Montreal Protocol mandates the phase-down of which class of chemical substances, primarily because of their extremely high global warming potential?

options.option_text: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) — already phased out under the original 1987 Protocol
Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) — potent synthetic greenhouse gases used in refrigeration
Perfluorocarbons (PFCs) — emitted mainly during aluminium smelting operations
Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) — phased out under earlier London and Beijing amendments

questions.explanation: B is correct: HFCs do not deplete the ozone layer (which is why they replaced CFCs/HCFCs) but have GWPs thousands of times higher than CO₂, making them potent climate threats. The Kigali Amendment specifically targets them. CFCs (A) were the original focus of the 1987 Protocol. HCFCs (D) were addressed through the London, Copenhagen, and Beijing amendments — not Kigali.

questions.stem: The Green Climate Fund (GCF), the primary UNFCCC financial mechanism to assist developing nations in climate adaptation and mitigation, was formally established at which Conference of Parties?

options.option_text: COP-15 in Copenhagen (2009) — produced the non-binding Copenhagen Accord
COP-16 in Cancun (2010) — established GCF under the Cancun Agreements
COP-17 in Durban (2011) — launched the Durban Platform for Enhanced Action
COP-18 in Doha (2012) — extended the Kyoto Protocol second commitment period

questions.explanation: B is correct: the GCF was established through the Cancun Agreements at COP16, Cancun, Mexico (2010). COP15 (Copenhagen) produced only a political accord without binding legal form. COP17 (Durban) created the Durban Platform that eventually led to the Paris Agreement. COP18 (Doha) extended Kyoto's second commitment period to 2020 — it did not create the GCF.

questions.stem: A key architectural difference between the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement is the nature of emission-reduction pledges. Which of the following best describes 'Nationally Determined Contributions' (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement?

options.option_text: Mandatory emissions quotas assigned to each country by the UNFCCC Secretariat
Self-determined climate action pledges submitted voluntarily by each member country
Financial commitments from developed nations deposited into the Green Climate Fund
Biennial emissions inventories submitted to the IPCC for global trend assessment

questions.explanation: B is correct: NDCs embody the Paris Agreement's 'bottom-up' architecture — each country self-determines its own pledge, unlike Kyoto's top-down legally binding targets assigned to Annex I countries. Option A describes how Kyoto worked, not Paris. Option C confuses NDCs with GCF financial pledges. Option D confuses NDCs with the Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs).

questions.stem: The 'Loss and Damage' fund — providing climate finance to countries suffering irreversible climate impacts beyond adaptation capacity — was formally agreed to be created at which COP?

options.option_text: COP-25 in Madrid, Spain (2019) — adopted the Chile-Madrid Time for Action
COP-26 in Glasgow, UK (2021) — produced the Glasgow Climate Pact agreement
COP-27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022) — agreed to establish a Loss and Damage fund
COP-28 in Dubai, UAE (2023) — concluded the first-ever Global Stocktake review

questions.explanation: C is correct: COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh (November 2022) was the breakthrough summit where parties formally agreed to establish a Loss and Damage fund for vulnerable nations. Glasgow (COP26, Option B) acknowledged the issue but failed to create a fund — a major point of contention. COP28 (Dubai, 2023) operationalized the fund but did not create it. Loss and Damage had been debated since 1991.

questions.stem: Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement creates a new international carbon crediting mechanism. Which Kyoto Protocol mechanism does it most directly succeed, allowing emission-reduction projects in developing countries to generate tradeable credits?

options.option_text: Joint Implementation (JI) — emission unit transfers between two Annex-I countries
Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) — credit generation from projects in developing nations
International Emissions Trading (IET) — direct swap of assigned amount units among parties
Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) — a domestic cap-and-trade system within Annex-B blocs

questions.explanation: B is correct: The CDM (Article 12, Kyoto Protocol) allowed developed (Annex I) countries to earn Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) by financing projects in developing countries — exactly the architecture that Article 6.4 replicates under the Paris framework. JI (A) was between two developed countries only. IET (C) was direct cap trading between Annex B parties. ETS (D) is a domestic mechanism, not a Kyoto flexibility mechanism.

questions.stem: The 'Global Stocktake' (GST) — the collective review mechanism under the Paris Agreement assessing overall progress toward its temperature and resilience goals — is mandated to occur at what periodicity?

options.option_text: Every three years, aligned with interim NDC progress reports under UNFCCC rules
Every five years, beginning 2023, to gauge collective Paris Agreement progress
Every two years, coinciding with Biennial Transparency Reports submitted by parties
Every ten years, linked to the IPCC Assessment Report cycle by formal convention

questions.explanation: B is correct: Article 14 of the Paris Agreement mandates a Global Stocktake every 5 years; the first concluded at COP28 (Dubai, December 2023). Its findings are meant to inform subsequent rounds of NDC updates. The 3-year option (A) is a tempting distractor since interim facilitative dialogues exist (e.g., Talanoa Dialogue 2018), but the formal GST cycle is 5 years. The 2-year cycle (C) describes Biennial Transparency Reports, a separate reporting obligation.
